nodes.label: The garage
nodes.rationale: Settings to Robot shows the robot's own account of itself: its name, a plan drawn to scale, and the specification it published. Nothing on it is typed in and nothing is configurable — it fills in on its own the moment a robot that publishes a sheet connects, and stays blank when one does not.

nodes.label: One line of adoption
nodes.rationale: RobotIdentity.declare("Ratchet") at the top of RobotContainer is the whole adoption. FrcCatalyst 1.10+ derives the team number, season, roboRIO serial and image, library and WPILib versions, brownout threshold, CAN inventory, gyro, and — once a SwerveSubsystem exists — drivetrain type, module count and positions, track width, wheelbase, odometry rate and top speed.

nodes.label: Derived rather than passed in
nodes.rationale: None of it is passed in, and that is the point. Anything passed in can drift: a team that regears its drive and forgets to edit an identity block publishes last month's robot with this month's confidence.

nodes.label: A builder for the facts no API can answer
nodes.rationale: A tape measure is the only source for a frame perimeter, and only your own build knows which commit the robot code came from. Everything in the builder is optional; leaving one out costs you that row and nothing else.

nodes.label: Gear ratios and mass are the exceptions
nodes.rationale: Gear ratios come only from the module constants handed to .swerveModules(...), because Phoenix builds a SwerveDrivetrain from them and will not hand them back. Mass and moment of inertia come from the deployed PathPlanner settings; a project without them publishes neither.

nodes.label: Nothing has to be republished
nodes.rationale: NT4 keeps the last value of every topic and hands it to whoever subscribes next, so a console that connects mid-match, or reconnects after the radio drops, gets the sheet on connect. The library rewrites it when a new source of facts turns up, so declaration order does not matter.

nodes.label: The nine spec sheet groups
nodes.rationale: Catalyst, Software, Controller, Drivetrain, Chassis, Traction, Power, Hardware, Power channels — the plan first, then the name with team, season and controller model, then the sheet grouped the way a spec sheet is read.

nodes.label: Bumper diagonal and channels used
nodes.rationale: Two rows are worked out here rather than read: the bumper diagonal, which is the width that has to clear a gap on the angle, and channels used, which counts the named channels against the module's total. Both are arithmetic on published figures, and both disappear when either side they are built from does.

nodes.label: A count and a list answer different questions
nodes.rationale: The count answers how loaded is the PDH; the list answers which breaker is the one that just popped, and only the robot knows that. The same reasoning splits the CAN tree out into its own Devices section: a count is the right shape for a glance and a tree is the right shape for a diagnosis.

nodes.label: The Catalyst group leads the sheet
nodes.rationale: It leads because it is the part that distinguishes robots. Two machines can have identical drivetrains and motor counts and be nothing alike, because one scores on its own and the other does not. Nothing in the group is declared — each entry is written by the component at the moment it is constructed. A list maintained by hand is a list of what a team meant to use; this is a list of what came up.

nodes.label: Why a missing fact is missing rather than dashed
nodes.rationale: Everywhere else an unpublished value shows a dash because the tile is a fixed shape. The sheet is the one place that rule points the other way. A dash on a Gyro row says this robot has no gyro; absence says it did not mention one, and only the second is ever true — the console cannot tell a robot without a gyro from a robot on an older library, or one whose sheet was written before the gyro was constructed.

nodes.label: The library omits rather than zeroes
nodes.rationale: A fact the library does not know is absent from the wire, not zero, not -1, not an empty string. Once a placeholder leaves the robot it is indistinguishable from a measurement. Rule 3 pushed back across the wire onto the robot side.

nodes.label: The plan, drawn from the wire
nodes.rationale: The bumper outline, the frame inside it, and a wheel at each published module position sized off the published wheel radius. Nose points up, which is +x in WPILib's frame. Drawn from measurements rather than picked from stock pictures because wrong dimensions look wrong: a team that published a 30-inch frame should see a 30-inch frame.

nodes.label: Partial figures give a partial drawing
nodes.rationale: With no bumper figures the outer edge is dashed; with no frame figures the deck is left out; with module positions alone the wheels sit inside a dashed outline taken from their own span; with none of the three there is no plan at all. The caption says what it was built from, so nobody reads one for the other.

nodes.label: The plan is not painted in the alliance colour
nodes.rationale: Alone among everything else on this dashboard that has bumpers. Alliance is match state: it flips between matches and a team carries both sets. A spec sheet that changed colour depending on when you opened it would be describing the match rather than the machine, and the machine is the same robot on either side.

nodes.label: Copy the spec sheet
nodes.rationale: Writes the whole thing to the clipboard as plain text in the selected units. At inspection someone is reading frame perimeter and weight off a screen and writing them onto a form; this is that without the transcription step. Written from the same data the panel rendered rather than derived a second time, so the text cannot disagree with the screen. If the clipboard refuses it says so rather than claiming a copy that did not happen.

nodes.label: The demo sheet is deliberately incomplete
nodes.rationale: No camera list, no drive ratio — because that is the ordinary case, and the panel leaving those lines out is the behaviour worth demonstrating. Named Demo robot so nobody mistakes it for their own.

nodes.label: The Settings panel, section by section
nodes.rationale: Everything the console lets you change about itself, in one panel. It replaced the modals that used to hang off the chips in the top strip and the About page with them. Opened with the gear or S; the link chip goes to Robot with the team field focused, L to Dashboard, and the wordmark, ? and F1 to About.

nodes.label: Nothing applies
nodes.rationale: There is no apply button and no confirmation step, because a control is the truth the moment you move it. The surface that changed a setting is responsible for making the board agree with it, and does so immediately.

nodes.label: Nothing is modal
nodes.rationale: No focus trap, no inert dashboard behind it, and the markup does not claim otherwise. It is a mode you step out of rather than a window that holds you — claiming modality would have been the markup saying one thing while the program did another.

nodes.label: It stands down
nodes.rationale: The moment the robot is enabled or E-stopped the panel closes itself along with anything else covering the board. Rule two: a driver who opened Settings in the pit and then got called to the field must not find the state lamp, the match timer and the E-stop indicator behind a panel.

nodes.label: Searching leaves matches where they live
nodes.rationale: Nothing is cloned into a results list — the row you find is the row itself, with the handler it was built with. The label, its explanation and any text on the control are all searched, so 'inches' finds Units, whose own word is 'Imperial'. A query that matches nothing says so, quoting what you typed. Escape clears the filter; a second Escape closes the panel. About holds prose rather than rows, so it never matches and never claims to.

nodes.label: The Devices section
nodes.rationale: The sheet answers what is this robot; this answers what is on it and where, which is a different question asked at a different time. CAN devices as a tree, one group per bus, needing FrcCatalyst 1.12+ which publishes Hardware/Devices as bus|id|type. Neither half is a setting, so neither is reachable by search.

nodes.label: The power board is drawn only from a published channel count
nodes.rationale: It appears only when the robot published a channel count — a strip sized to whatever happens to be in use would be inventing the shape of a distribution board nobody described. Rule 3 applied to a drawing rather than to a number.

nodes.label: Trail length applies on release
nodes.rationale: Applied on release rather than during the drag, because the trail buffer is allocated when the scene is built, so changing the length is a rebuild.

nodes.label: One camera, two surfaces, one function
nodes.rationale: The buttons in the tile's own corner move the same setting as the Settings row; there is one camera and both surfaces go through one function to change it, because a tile quietly holding a camera of its own is how the two came to disagree.

nodes.label: Opens on applies at launch only
nodes.rationale: Setting it does not switch the view now, because that would be the setting acting on the wrong occasion.

nodes.label: An import is checked whole before anything is applied
nodes.rationale: A document with one bad tile is refused with the reason, and the board on screen is left alone. A half-applied layout would be worse than a refused one.

nodes.label: Reset arms itself rather than opening a dialog
nodes.rationale: Two presses rather than a dialog — the button arms itself and disarms after four seconds — because rule two says nothing blocks the board.

nodes.label: Alert hold
nodes.rationale: How long a cleared alert stays on screen, dimmed, 0 to 8 s. Applied live on the drag since nothing has to be rebuilt. Robot alerts sitting near their threshold raise and clear repeatedly, and a tile that strobes next to a driver is worse than useless.

nodes.label: Demo data is amber, alone among the switches
nodes.rationale: Off by default and never remembered, the dock button stays lit the whole time it runs, and switching it on stands this panel down exactly as a robot enabling does. A dashboard that quietly invents telemetry is a hazard, so every part of that is deliberate. The duplicate switch in the dock is on purpose: while demo runs the fact that the numbers are invented has to be visible on the dashboard itself.

nodes.label: Release notes are shown as plain text, never rendered
nodes.rationale: The notes are shown before you decide rather than after — the page is a decision rather than a changelog. The text arrived over the network, so it is shown as plain text and never rendered as markup.

nodes.label: About lays the three rules across on a wide window
nodes.rationale: On a window 1080px or wider the three rules sit side by side rather than stacked, so they are read across rather than scrolled through: they are one idea in three parts, and a reader who has to scroll to reach the third has stopped holding the first two. Narrower than that it folds back to one column.

nodes.label: Frames counts real NetworkTables frames only
nodes.rationale: Demo ticks are not NetworkTables frames, and counting them would be the console inventing a number about itself. Rule 3 turned inward on the console's own diagnostics.

nodes.label: Bundled but switched off says exactly that
nodes.rationale: A model that is bundled but switched off reports itself as such, rather than reporting a preference as a fact about the build.

nodes.label: Every binding is a single unmodified key
nodes.rationale: A driver station is operated under pressure and often without looking down. That is exactly why typing in any field suspends them all: a bare d must never toggle demo data while somebody is halfway through typing a topic path. Escape in a field means abandon what I am typing and blurs it; a second Escape closes what is open.

nodes.label: Storage is read one key at a time and every key is checked
nodes.rationale: A number outside its range is pulled back into it and anything else falls back to the default, because storage can hold anything — an older build wrote it, someone edited it by hand, a quota error truncated it — and a bad value out of there lands in a component that has no business validating a setting. Everything lives in local storage except the team number, which belongs to the backend because the MCP server has to read it with no webview involved.

nodes.label: The widget catalogue
nodes.rationale: Every tile binds to NetworkTables keys you choose, so none of it is hard-coded to a season or a robot. Grouped as Match, Telemetry, Health, Field and Pit.

nodes.label: The component registry
nodes.rationale: The registry in src/app.js takes a config schema, a render that builds DOM once, and an update called each frame.

nodes.label: update must be cheap and must not throw
nodes.rationale: One bad tile cannot be allowed to take out the board, and the paint loop enforces that. The registry contract as an expression of rule 2.

nodes.label: Alerts are held after they clear
nodes.rationale: Held for a couple of seconds after they clear, dimmed. Anything edge-triggered on a measurement sitting near its threshold raises and clears repeatedly, and rendering that verbatim gives a tile that strobes next to a driver.

nodes.label: The chase camera swings around occluding field elements
nodes.rationale: Rather than leaving you looking at the back of a truss.
